title: Reliability Tryathon: experiment slate and stakeholder rally
body:
Purpose
This doc captures the plan for a 2-week cross-functional 'Reliability Tryathon' — a focused set of small, hypothesis-driven experiments intended to validate SLO design choices, telemetry gaps, and mitigation patterns for model-serving surfaces. Goal: surface which reliability levers materially improve our customer-impacting signals and which introduce unintended customer regressions.

Why a Tryathon (notes to self)
- We need fast, measurable probes instead of long, risky rollouts.
- Focus on cheap, reversible experiments where possible (config changes, routing rules, canary policies, cache tweaks).
- Create a repeatable pattern so feature teams can run their own mini-tryathons later.

Scope and constraints
- Services in scope: hosted inference API (text generation), embeddings, and dedicated inference routing.
- Exclude: private on-prem deployments for this run (network/regulatory test cost too high).
- Constraint: experiments must be reversible within a single release window (~2 business days).
- Safety gate: any change that increases error-rate above 0.2% in a 15-minute window must be auto-rolled.

Timeline (high level)
- Week 0 (planning): intake, finalize slate, allocate infra tokens, post to #sre-tryathon. (Aug 3–7)
- Week 1 (run experiments): small config changes, routing policy probes, telemetry increments (Aug 10–14)
- Week 2 (analysis + handoff): collect metrics, runbook sketches, decide follow-ups (Aug 17–21)

Stakeholders & communication
- Convener: Aisha Patel (SRE)
- Product partner: Priya Nair (product-hosted-api)
- Applied ML liaison: Miguel Santos (applied-ml)
- Platform/Infra: Tomoko Yamada (platform-engineering)
- Oncall support: roster from SRE rotation; point person Ethan Liu
- Weekly sync cadence: daily 20-min stand during run week; final 60-min retrospective; optional office hours 30m daily.
- Slack channel: #sre-tryathon (use thread per experiment); escalate in #ops-escalations if roll trigger hit.

Experiment Slate (intake entries)
1) KV-prefix caching warm window change
   - Hypothesis: Increasing prefix cache TTL from 60s->300s for common prompt prefixes will reduce tail latency and token compute cost for chat infrequently mutated prefixes.
   - Metric(s): p95 token latency, tokens/sec billed, cache hit ratio by prefix class, tail CPU utilization on GPU hosts.
   - Owner: Tomoko Yamada
   - Success criteria: p95 latency drop >= 8% for calls with cached prefixes and no increase in 99th percentile generation latency for uncached calls > 3%.
   - Risk & rollback: if global token-cost rises or 5xxs rise > 0.1% absolute, revert TTL within 15 minutes. 

2) Canary routing to quantized model variant for low-priority traffic
   - Hypothesis: Routing 5% of low-priority requests to a quantized variant reduces cost without user-visible degradation for rerank/summary workloads.
   - Metric(s): relative generation quality via BLEU/ROUGE proxy on saved prompts, per-request latency change, error rate, cost-per-token delta.
   - Owner: Miguel Santos
   - Success criteria: no measurable quality regression on our canned prompt set (automated eval pass rate >= 95%), cost-per-token improvement >= 12%.
   - Risk & rollback: immediate rollback if user-reported regressions (support ticket inflow) or automated eval fail rate > 5%.

3) Batching policy stress test (dynamic batch size cap)
   - Hypothesis: Increasing max batch size during low-latency windows improves throughput with acceptable latency tail for interactive apps.
   - Metric(s): latency SLO p50/p95/p99, throughput, model GPU saturation, queued-request counts.
   - Owner: Ethan Liu
   - Success criteria: throughput uplift >= 18% with p95 increase <= 12ms and p99 increase <= 30ms.
   - Risk & rollback: reduce max batch size if p99 increases beyond threshold or observed QoS violations.

4) Trace enrichment for generation-side errors
   - Hypothesis: Adding context (prompt length, truncated tokens, model-variant tag) to error traces reduces MTTR by enabling faster root cause and fewer back-and-forths with product owners.
   - Metric(s): MTTR (median time to ticket triage and first actionable debug step), fraction of incidents needing model engineering involvement.
   - Owner: Priya Nair
   - Success criteria: median MTTR improvement >= 20% and fewer full-model-engineer wakeups over the week.
   - Risk & rollback: privacy review — must ensure no user PII shipped. Stop enrichment if privacy scan flags.

Candidate SLOs to validate (experiments will inform thresholds)
- SLO A (interactive-generation latency): p95 end-to-end generation latency <= 350ms for signed-in dev tier (target test dataset), error budget 99.9% availability.
- SLO B (embedding service availability): 99.95% successful request rate (exclude 4xxs from client misuse).
- SLO C (model-serving correctness): automated eval pass-rate on synthetic prompt set >= 98% for production variants (non-customer-facing regression detection).
Notes: These are intentionally provisional. The tryathon is designed to supply real-world delta numbers to set realistic thresholds and error budgets.

Measurement & telemetry checklist
- Ensure buckets exist: p50/p90/p95/p99 for latency, per-route; error counts (4xx/5xx) per model variant; token counts per request; cost estimation per minute.
- Short-term dashboards to spin up: tryathon/kv-caching, tryathon/canary-quant, tryathon/batching, tryathon/trace-enrich.
- Logging retention: increase short-term retention to 7 days for enriched traces (default 3d) for faster triage.

Runbook sketch (templates to be produced during run week)
- Each experiment must declare: rollback steps (1–3), who triggers rollback, monitoring query to validate, and safe ramp schedule.
- Example rollback step (canary quantized): route 5% -> 0% in routing table; redeploy routing-config; confirm rollback with 5-min window health check.

Risk heatmap (quick scan)
- High risk: routing to unknown model variants (quality regressions), experiment-induced spike in token-cost.
- Medium risk: telemetry explosions (too many traces causing SLO breaches on observability), intermittent latency spikes from batching mis-tuning.
- Low risk: configuration-only changes that are reversible automatically via feature-flag.

Post-run deliverables
- Experiment results doc (structured): baseline vs experiment numbers, signal graphs, lesson learned, recommendation (discard, adopt, scale pilot).
- SLO proposal update: use measured p95/p99 deltas to set concrete SLO targets and error budgets for Q4 planning.
- Runbook additions: common rollback patterns and standard monitoring queries added to the SRE runbook library.
- Handoff: any persistent changes promoted via a product PR and cross-org signoff template.

Open questions (to resolve in planning)
- How much traffic can product afford to label as "low-priority" for canary routing? We need product threshold. (action: Priya)
- Are there billing/chargeback implications from temporarily higher token usage during tests? (action: finance ask: @Megan in finance)
- Privacy signoff for trace enrichment: confirm allowed fields and redaction process. (action: security review)

Next steps (this doc is the intake artifact)
- Fill the REL-913 intake rows with the experiment configs (owners by Aug 6).
- Convene 30-min pre-run sync to finalize dashboards (Aug 7).
- During the run: post daily status to #sre-tryathon and update the shared experiment tracker.

Appendix: quick links and artifacts
- Intake tracker: JIRA REL-913
- Tryathon landing page (short): Confluence /display/RELIABILITY/Tryathon-Overview
- Example monitoring queries: use queries from tryathon/query-templates (temporary dashboard kit).

Notes to self (informal)
- Keep experiments small, reversible. Aim for 2–3 measurable knobs per day instead of big lifts.
- Document every rollback even if unused — that helps future teams trust the pattern.
- If something surprises us (positive or negative), capture all raw traces for offline analysis before reverting.

End of doc.
